title: The dead philosophers
hook: Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates: all gone, and all did their work (Meditations 6.47)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on loving the portion you were given, truly and sincerely. Your line was love these people.

The stones in an old cemetery read like a town meeting: a doctor, a schoolteacher, a child, a soldier, somebody's beloved grandmother. Each one was the center of a whole world, and now the names are fading in the rain. It can feel crushing. Or it can feel like company. Marcus Aurelius took that walk in his head, in book six, and the stones he read had some very famous names on them.

In Meditations six, forty-seven, Marcus tells himself to keep in mind that people of every kind, every trade and every nation have died. Then he names them. Great speakers. Noble philosophers: Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates. Heroes of old days, generals and tyrants. Then the sharp minds: Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Archimedes, men of keen natural talent, as he puts it. All in the dust, he says, where we're all going. These aren't strangers to him; he names Heraclitus and Socrates elsewhere in the Meditations too. Remembering that even they died doesn't shrink them. It puts him in their line. If Socrates had to die, Marcus can stop acting as if he won't. Then the turn: what's left that's worth a great deal? To live through life in truth and justice, and to be kindly even toward liars and the unjust. The dead philosophers didn't escape death. They did their work, and in Marcus's sense that's the part that lasts: it was done. Every one of us is downstream of someone who taught us and is gone. A grandparent who explained how to be honest. A teacher who saw something in you. A writer you read once at nineteen. Remembering them on purpose is a practice Marcus kept: book one of the Meditations is Marcus thanking, one by one, the people who formed him.
screen: `EVERY KIND OF PERSON HAS DIED.` · `HERACLITUS, PYTHAGORAS, SOCRATES.` · `WHAT'S WORTH MUCH: TRUTH, JUSTICE.` · `REMEMBER YOUR OWN DEAD TEACHERS.` · then, large: `THEY DID THEIR WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one teacher of yours who has died, a relative, a mentor, an author, and recall one thing they taught you, in words or by example. Say their name quietly and thank them in whatever way is natural for you. Then rest in the plain fact that some of their work is in you now.
Archimedes, one of the sharp minds Marcus names among the dead, all in the dust where we're all going, and what remained was their work. Today's word.
Your line: they did their work. Truth and justice, lived while there's time, are what's worth much. That's day five hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus keep a habit like his book one: naming and thanking the teachers, living and dead, who formed them, and remembering that the great ones also died after doing their work.
